title: The Stronger Material That Made the Heavier Tie Rod
featured_title: THE STRONGER MATERIAL THAT MADE THE HEAVIER TIE ROD
subject: other-disciplines

presentation.challenge: Material A had the higher yield strength, but its density penalty was much larger. After sizing both rods to the same factor of safety, Material B produced the lighter design.

practice.primary_question: How should yield strength and density be combined when selecting a minimum-mass material for a strength-limited tie rod?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Choosing the material with the highest yield strength without accounting for density and the cross-sectional area required by allowable stress.

case_dna.target_misconception: The material with the highest yield strength always gives the lightest strength-limited member.
case_dna.why_plausible: Higher strength reduces required area, but mass also depends on density.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For a 60 kN, 1 m tie rod with FS=2, Material A needs 400 mm² and weighs 3.12 kg; Material B needs 500 mm² but weighs only 1.35 kg.
case_dna.corrected_model: For a tension member sized by allowable stress, mass is proportional to rho/sigma_allow, so strength and density must be considered together.

problem_statement: A 1.0 m tie rod must carry 60 kN in tension with factor of safety 2 against yielding. Material A has yield strength 300 MPa and density 7800 kg/m³. Material B has yield strength 240 MPa and density 2700 kg/m³. Neglect connection mass. Determine the minimum required area and mass for each material and select the lighter design.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Higher yield strength did not guarantee lower mass.
gates.prompt: What property besides allowable stress affects member mass?

options.label: Size area from P/sigma_allow, then compare rho A L
options.reason: Mass depends on both required area and density.

options.label: Choose the highest yield strength only
Choose the lowest density without checking strength
options.reason: The design must first satisfy the allowable-stress constraint.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Size both tie rods
gates.result: Material B produces the lighter feasible tie rod at about 1.35 kg.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove Material B mass
gates.prompt: Use sigma_allow=240/2=120 MPa, A=60000/120e6, and m=rho A L. Enter kg.

cards.text: A: sigma_allow=150 MPa, area=400 mm², mass=3.12 kg.
B: sigma_allow=120 MPa, area=500 mm², mass=1.35 kg.
B needs 25% more area but is about 57% lighter.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the material-selection note
report: C1. Material A has higher yield strength.
C2. Higher strength reduces required area.
C3. Therefore Material A must produce the lighter rod.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: A does have higher yield strength.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores A's much higher density.

evidence_choices.label: mA=3.12 kg versus mB=1.35 kg
evidence_choices.reason: The actual mass comparison includes both area and density.

correction.template: Material {material} is lighter at about {mass_kg} kg.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Identify the useful screening metric
gates.constraint: Same load, length, and factor of safety for candidate materials.

options.label: Maximize yield strength divided by density
options.reason: For this strength-limited geometry, mass scales with rho/Sy when FS is common.

options.label: Minimize density only
options.reason: Strength must also satisfy the load.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Evaluate a third material
gates.prompt: Material C has Sy=180 MPa and rho=1800 kg/m³. With the same P, L, and FS, what mass is required?

options.label: 2.00 kg
options.reason: That does not follow allowable-stress sizing.

gates.explanation: For each candidate, size the required area first, then multiply by density and length.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the material selection
gates.confirmation: I confirm that minimum-mass strength-limited material selection must consider both allowable strength and density.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Highest yield strength was treated as the only selection criterion.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Size by allowable stress, then compare rho A L or use strength-to-density as a screening metric.

seo.seo_title: Material Selection by Strength-to-Density | FE Other Disciplines E-100
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Other Disciplines E-100: the higher-strength material makes a 3.12 kg tie rod, while the lower-density alternative needs 1.35 kg.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE material selection strength to density
seo.excerpt: The strongest material is not always the lightest design. Density and required area must be evaluated together.
seo.direct_answer: With FS=2, Material A needs 400 mm² and has mass 3.12 kg. Material B needs 500 mm² but has mass only 1.35 kg, so B is the lighter strength-compliant choice.

faqs.q: What screening metric helps minimize mass in a strength-limited tie rod?
faqs.a: For common geometry and safety factor, maximize yield strength divided by density.
